analysis.title: From Rotation To Rout (Investor Positioning and Flows)
key_insights: The October rotation out of Tech from extended levels has widened into a broad rout. Cited catalysts are a US mid-term blue wave, issues surrounding NVDA, fears of large equity supply and a number of concurrent tech outages. The S&P 500 is down more than 10% from its recent peak.

S&P 500 pullbacks of 3% to 5% occur every 2-3 months. Pullbacks of 10% occur about once a year and are usually tied to clear shocks or significant growth concerns (Liberation Day, 2022 Fed hiking fears).

Aggregate equity positioning is -0.9sd (11th percentile), near the bottom of its +/-1sd band and the lowest since May 2025. It is now low in absolute terms, not only relative to earnings growth, and approaches levels from which it has typically bounced.
Discretionary positioning is at -0.95sd (5th percentile). Systematic positioning fell from neutral last week to -0.85sd (16th percentile), its biggest underweight in 18 months.

Pricing and positioning are consistent with an outright contraction in S&P 500 earnings and ISM and global manufacturing PMIs well below 50. The median post-war recession decline in the S&P 500 is -24%, so the current selloff is about halfway there.

A vol shock is underway. Implied and realized volatility, intra-day ranges, VIX futures curve inversion and implied correlations are all in the top decile, a jump of more than 1.5sd. This forces selling by systematic strategies directly and by discretionary investors indirectly.
In past vol shocks, vol took an average of 6 to 8 weeks to subside and equities to bottom. The S&P 500 fell 14% to 16% on average in episodes outside recessions and took 4 to 6 months to recoup.

Tech is at the bottom of its decade-long channel on an absolute basis and well below the channel relative to the rest of the S&P 500. The last time it was at the bottom of the absolute channel was end-March (Iran war selloff). Relative levels are last seen around Liberation Day.
The Nasdaq 100 is more than 10% below its 200dma, only the 5th such occurrence in the last decade (end-2018, pandemic start, 2022, Liberation Day).

Sector positioning: Energy is notably overweight (0.62sd, 91st percentile) and Healthcare overweight (0.24sd, 64th). MCG & Tech is modestly underweight (-0.23sd, 21st). Financials are neutral (-0.02sd, 42nd). Materials (11th) and Consumer Cyclicals (13th) are significantly underweight. Consumer Staples (5th) is below its range and Utilities (2nd) is at an extreme.

Options: the call-to-put volume ratio fell to the 32nd percentile, led by lower net call volume in MCG & Tech single-stock options. S&P 500 3m 90-110 skew rose. The highest-net-call-volume basket and the most-shorted basket both underperformed this week.
AAII sentiment (bull minus bear) rose but remained bearish for a sixth straight week (21st percentile). Bearish responses are at the 85th percentile.

Systematic detail: vol-control equity allocation is at the 21st percentile. CTA equity allocation is at the 36th percentile, a seven-month low. CTA long positioning in US large caps is at a seven-month low and short positioning in US small caps is at a 16-month high. Risk parity cut equities (56th percentile) and added bonds and inflation-linked notes.
CTA long USD positioning is at the 97th percentile, rising toward extremes. CTA oil longs (74th percentile) were trimmed and gold shorts were covered slightly.

Fund flows: equity fund inflows were $66.6bn, a three-week low but still very robust. US received $45.6bn and global funds $15.1bn. EM inflows were $8.3bn, a six-week low. Japan saw outflows of $4.2bn.
Sector funds: Tech took $5.4bn, its eighth straight week of inflows at a slower pace. Industrials had record outflows of $2.3bn. Materials, Financials and Energy also had outflows.

Bond funds had outflows of $7.4bn, the first since Liberation Day (April 2025). EM bond funds lost $7.5bn, the biggest outflow since March 2020. Money market funds took $0.4bn, with Europe seeing $25.4bn of outflows.
DB S&P 500 forecasts: 2026 target 8000, 2026 EPS $362, 2027 EPS $430.

earnings_insights: DB's S&P 500 2026 EPS forecast is $362 and 2027 EPS forecast is $430 (forecast).

Equity positioning is now in line with an outright contraction in S&P 500 earnings, and large-cap positioning has a 49% correlation with S&P 500 EPS growth (2012-2025). Positioning also has a 42% correlation with the EPS revision ratio since 2012, and the report presents positioning as consistent with earnings downgrades.
Recent DB earnings publications (Nov 6) describe Q3 2026 global earnings as broad-based strength, and a Nov 2 note says growth holds in the 30s.

vol_and_positioning: A vol shock (a jump of more than 1.5sd) is underway: implied vol, realized vol, intra-day ranges, VIX futures curve inversion and implied correlations are all in the top decile.
Past vol shocks took 6-8 weeks on average for vol to subside and equities to bottom. The S&P 500 fell 14-16% on average outside recessions and took 4-6 months to recover.
Aggregate equity positioning is -0.90sd (11th percentile). Discretionary is -0.95sd (5th percentile) and systematic is -0.85sd (16th percentile).
Vol-control funds cut equity allocation again (21st percentile), and their sensitivity to further selloffs rose modestly.

CTA equity allocation is at the 36th percentile, a seven-month low. Nasdaq 100 positioning (15th) is slightly short, US large cap longs (18th) are at a seven-month low, and US small cap shorts (9th) are at a 16-month high.
The call/put volume ratio is at the 32nd percentile and S&P 500 3m 90-110 skew rose this week.
Futures positioning data is as of Nov 10, while other positioning data is as of Nov 18-19.
geopolitical: US mid-term blue wave cited as a negative catalyst for equities.
Iran war selloff at the end of March is cited as the last time Tech was at the bottom of its absolute channel.
